Analyzing US Census Data by Chloe Mercurio

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(sf)
```

Every ACS request comes down to three choices: the **geographic level** (county here, but census tract, place, or state are also available), the **variables** (Census table codes like `B19013_001` for median household income), and the **year**. For the ACS, `year = 2020` retrieves the 2016–2020 5-year estimates, pooled across five years so even small counties have reliable numbers.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| cache: true
income_tx <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = "B19013_001",
  state = "TX",
  year = 2020,
  geometry = TRUE
)
```

```{r}
#| message: false
edu_state <- get_acs(
  geography = "state",
  variables = c("B15003_001", "B15003_022", "B15003_023", "B15003_024", "B15003_025"),
  summary_var = "B15003_001",
  year = 2020
)
```

```{r}
#| message: false
age_ca <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(median_age = "B01002_001", population = "B01003_001"),
  state = "CA",
  year = 2020,
  geometry = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
age_ca |>
  select(NAME, variable, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = estimate) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = B01003_001, y = B01002_001)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "County Population and Median Age in California",
    x = "Population (log scale)",
    y = "Median age (years)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
edu_state |>
  filter(variable %in% c("B15003_022", "B15003_023", "B15003_024", "B15003_025")) |>
  group_by(GEOID, NAME) |>
  summarise(
    bachelors_or_higher = sum(estimate) / first(summary_est) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, bachelors_or_higher), y = bachelors_or_higher)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Bachelor's Degree or Higher by State",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Population age 25+ with a bachelor's degree or higher"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
ggplot(income_tx) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = estimate), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "viridis",
    labels = scales::label_dollar(),
    name = "Median household income\n(USD)"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Household Income by Texas County",
    caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2016-2020 American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates."
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_text(color = "gray40", hjust = 0)
  )
```

```{r}
ggplot(income_tx) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = estimate), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "cividis",
    labels = scales::label_dollar(),
    name = "Median household income\n(USD)"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Household Income by Texas County (Cividis)",
    caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2016-2020 American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates."
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_text(color = "gray40", hjust = 0)
  )
```

Every county arrives with a `GEOID` (its FIPS code), a `NAME`, the `variable` code, an `estimate`, and a margin of error (`moe`). The `estimate` is the survey's best guess. The `moe` is the half-width of its 90% confidence interval.

`income_tx` contains 254 Texas counties, each with an income estimate, its margin of error, and the polygon used to draw it on the map.

After a successful render, `analysis_cache/` sits next to `analysis_files/` and holds the saved `income_tx`, including its polygons. Later renders can use the cached result instead of repeating the Census API call and boundary download.
